domain_label: Study System — Spaced-Repetition Algorithms as the Compute Core (SM-2 / classic Anki / FSRS-6)
purpose: A method for the computational steps an expert reasons about when choosing and tuning a spaced-repetition scheduler: the SM-2 update math (E-Factor, interval ladder, 0-5 quality grades, floor 1.3), how classic Anki deviates (learning steps, 4-button ease deltas, lapse/leech, late-answer credit, multipliers, mandatory fuzz), the FSRS-6 DSR model (difficulty/stability/retrievability, the trainable power forgetting curve, the 21-parameter w-vector and its per-user revlog optimization), and the desired-retention-vs-workload trade that sets the single workload knob — each step sourced honestly against the grounding file's FACT/ESTIMATE/UNKNOWN tags, never inventing a formula, constant or effect size the research did not verify.
assumptions: no live per-user revlog or benchmark dataset is supplied; every score is a heuristic prior and every algorithm constant is quoted from the grounding research file's fetched sources (Anki source, FSRS wiki, SM-2 mirror), not re-derived here

the SM-2 formula text is taken from a verbatim GitHub mirror cross-matched against 26 independent mirrors because the canonical supermemo.com page was unreachable this session (egress 403); the algorithm is treated as FACT-by-cross-match with the original-page-not-directly-fetched caveat carried

FSRS-6 formulas and the 21-parameter default vector are quoted from the official open-spaced-repetition algorithm wiki fetched this session; parameter values are defaults, not a fit to any specific user
grade vocabularies differ by family (SM-2 uses 0-5, Anki/FSRS use 1-4) and are only reconciled at import boundaries, never silently equated

primary psychology effect sizes (Ebbinghaus, Cepeda 2006, Roediger 2006 exact numbers) were unreachable (journals/Wikipedia blocked) and are held UNKNOWN; only the two fetched quantitative findings (Rea & Modigliani 70% vs 53%, Donovan & Radosevich effect size 0.46) are stated as FACT
exclusions: the file-format / database / HTTP integration surface (.apkg/.colpkg, the SQLite notes/cards/revlog/col schema, AnkiConnect actions, genanki .apkg generation) beyond the revlog tuple shape the optimizer consumes; that transport-and-storage layer belongs to the integration specialist and is not collapsed into the compute core
content authoring, card/note design, cloze construction and item atomicity beyond SM-2's 'smallest possible items' precondition
UI/UX of study sessions, queue ordering, daily new/review limits and burying/siblings scheduling beyond the per-card state transition math
restating a fabricated algorithm constant, an unpublished FSRS parameter value, or a primary-source effect size the grounding file marked UNKNOWN as if it were fetched fact
sync protocol, media handling, and multi-device conflict resolution

glossary.definition: The framing that any spaced-repetition scheduler is a pure map (grade, elapsed_time) -> (next memory state, next interval); response-dependence (the grade) and time-dependence (elapsed days) are both mandatory inputs. fsrs-rs exposes this literally as next_states(previous_memory_state, desired_retention, elapsed_days) [FACT - fsrs-rs README].

SM-2's per-item ease multiplier, initialized 2.5, updated after every repetition by EF' = EF + (0.1 - (5-q)*(0.08 + (5-q)*0.02)) and floored at 1.3; the interval after the second repetition grows geometrically as I(n)=I(n-1)*EF [FACT - SM-2 mirror cross-matched against 26 GitHub mirrors; canonical supermemo.com page unreachable this session].

SM-2's response grade: 5 perfect, 4 correct after hesitation, 3 correct with serious difficulty, 2 incorrect but correct answer easy to recall, 1 incorrect with correct answer remembered, 0 complete blackout; q<3 triggers a ladder reset [FACT - SM-2 mirror]. Anki collapses this to 4 buttons (Again/Hard/Good/Easy) with one fail grade [FACT - Anki FAQ].

The minimum ease/E-Factor both SM-2 and Anki enforce (SM-2 EF>=1.3; Anki MINIMUM_EASE_FACTOR=1.3, INITIAL_EASE_FACTOR=2.5); Anki's FAQ cites SuperMemo research that eases below 130% make cards due more often than useful [FACT - review.rs lines 16-17 + Anki FAQ].

FSRS's three-component memory state: Difficulty D in [1,10] (how hard it is to raise S), Stability S (days for R to decay 100%->90%, i.e. the interval at which R=90%), and Retrievability R (probability of recall now, the only component that changes without a review) [FACT - FSRS FAQ + algorithm wiki].

FSRS-6's trainable recall curve R(t,S) = (1 + factor*t/S)^(-w20) with factor = 0.9^(-1/w20)-1 chosen so R(S,S)=0.9; its inverse gives the next interval I(r,S) = (S/factor)*(r^(-1/w20)-1) with I(0.9,S)=S. (FSRS-4.5/5 fixed DECAY=-0.5, FACTOR=19/81; v4 used DECAY=-1, FACTOR=1/9.) [FACT - FSRS algorithm wiki].

FSRS-6's parameters w0..w20: w0..w3 initial stability per grade, w4/w5 initial difficulty, w6/w7 difficulty update and mean reversion, w8..w16 success-stability terms, w11..w14 lapse-stability, w15/w16 hard/easy stability multipliers, w17..w19 same-day review, w20 the forgetting-curve decay; fit per user to the revlog [FACT - FSRS algorithm wiki + mechanism-of-optimization wiki].

The single dial r that sets interval = inverse forgetting curve at r; r=0.90 default, above 0.90 workload rises quickly and above 0.97 it becomes overwhelming; the workload-vs-retention curve is U-shaped (higher r -> shorter intervals -> more reviews; lower r -> more forgetting -> more relearning) with a minimum found by Anki's CMRR [FACT - deck-options.md + optimal-retention wiki].

The FSRS property that for an overdue-but-recalled card the stability increase converges to an upper bound rather than growing linearly with the interval as SM-2/Anki do; SInc = S'/S >= 1, shrinks with higher D and higher S, and grows as R drops (the spacing effect encoded directly) [FACT - FSRS algorithm wiki].

The one-row-per-review tuple (epoch-ms timestamp, card id, grade/button 1-4, new interval, previous interval, review duration ms, type 0=learn/1=review/2=relearn/3=cram) that is exactly what the FSRS optimizer consumes and what Anki's insertReviews imports; logging it from day one keeps every scheduler retunable [FACT - Anki DB schema + AnkiConnect README].

nodes.definition: Compute the SM-2 E-Factor update, the core of the oldest family. Each item starts at EF=2.5; after every repetition EF is updated by EF' = EF + (0.1 - (5-q)*(0.08 + (5-q)*0.02)), then floored: if EF' < 1.3 then EF' := 1.3 [FACT - SM-2 mirror cross-matched against 26 GitHub mirrors]. The resulting per-grade deltas are q=5 +0.10, q=4 0.00, q=3 -0.14, q=2 -0.32, q=1 -0.54, q=0 -0.80 [FACT by arithmetic]. Note the update runs on EVERY repetition including a failure (step 5), independent of the interval reset (step 6). nodes.definition: Compute the SM-2 interval ladder that turns EF into a schedule. I(1) := 1 day, I(2) := 6 days, and for n>2 I(n) := I(n-1)*EF, with fractional intervals rounded UP to the nearest integer [FACT - SM-2 mirror]. Interval growth is therefore geometric in EF: with EF held at the 1.3 floor the interval only ever grows 1.3x per step, while at EF=2.5 it grows 2.5x. The first two rungs are fixed constants, not EF-scaled, so EF only governs the schedule from the third repetition onward. This ladder plus the EF update is the entire scheduling behavior of textbook SM-2 for a card that never fails.

nodes.definition: Handle an SM-2 failure precisely, because the two effects are commonly conflated. If q<3, repetitions restart from the beginning of the ladder (I(1), I(2), ...) WITHOUT changing EF [FACT - SM-2 mirror step 6]. But the EF update of step 5 still ran on that same repetition, so a failure lowers EF (e.g. q=0 gives -0.80) even though the reset itself does not touch EF. Additionally, at the end of each day's session SM-2 re-repeats all items that scored <4 until every one scores >=4. The precise reading: failure resets POSITION on the ladder (n back to 1) while the grade independently moves EF; treating the reset as 'EF unchanged on failure' is the classic misimplementation.

nodes.definition: Name SM-2's central blind spot: it schedules from (EF, n) alone and ignores how much time ACTUALLY elapsed between reviews. A card answered on time and a card answered a month late get the same next interval, because the ladder multiplies the planned interval by EF regardless of the real delay [FACT by definition of the ladder]. This is the design gap the two later families each address differently: classic Anki patches it ad hoc by crediting days_late into the next interval, while FSRS handles it natively because R(t,S) takes elapsed time as a first-class input and yields a bounded, principled stability gain for overdue-but-recalled cards [FACT - Anki FAQ + FSRS algorithm wiki]. Recognizing this blindness is what motivates choosing or patching a scheduler.

nodes.definition: Model classic Anki's first deviation: user-configurable learning steps replace SM-2's fixed 1d/6d rungs. The default steps are 1m 10m; a card graduates to review after passing the last step [FACT - Anki deck-options + FAQ]. Crucially, failures DURING learning do not touch the card's ease - 'the initial acquisition process does not influence a card's ease' - which deliberately avoids 'low interval hell' where early stumbles permanently depress ease [FACT - Anki FAQ]. This is the exact opposite convention to SM-2, where a failed repetition still runs the EF-lowering update. The learning phase is thus a soft on-ramp before the SM-2-style ease/interval machinery takes over at graduation.

nodes.definition: Establish the FSRS DSR memory model, the compute core of the modern scheduler Anki ships (since 23.10) and descends from MaiMemo's DHP / Wozniak's three-component model [FACT - FSRS FAQ + fsrs-rs README]. Grades are G: 1 again, 2 hard, 3 good, 4 easy. Each card carries its own (D, S) memory state and R is computed from S and elapsed time, never stored. This triple is what every FSRS formula reads and writes.

nodes.definition: Compute the FSRS-6 forgetting curve and its inverse. The recall curve is a power law with trainable decay: R(t,S) = (1 + factor * t/S)^(-w20), where factor = 0.9^(-1/w20) - 1 is chosen so that R(S,S) = 0.9 (by construction the card's recall is 90% exactly when elapsed time equals its stability) [FACT - FSRS algorithm wiki]. The next interval for a desired retention r is the inverse of the curve: I(r,S) = (S/factor) * (r^(-1/w20) - 1), giving I(0.9, S) = S. FSRS-4.5/5 fixed DECAY=-0.5 and FACTOR=19/81; FSRS v4 used DECAY=-1 and FACTOR=1/9; FSRS-6 makes the decay w20 trainable [FACT - FSRS wiki]. This power curve (not an exponential) is the mathematical heart that makes elapsed time first-class.

nodes.definition: Compute the FSRS difficulty update after a review, designed against 'ease hell' via linear damping and mean reversion. The raw change is dD = -w6*(G-3), so grades above Good lower difficulty and below Good raise it. Apply linear damping toward the extremes: D' = D + dD*(10-D)/9. Then mean-revert toward the Easy-anchored initial difficulty: D'' = w7*D0(4) + (1-w7)*D', and clamp to [1,10] [FACT - FSRS algorithm wiki]. The mean reversion is what stops difficulty from ratcheting monotonically to an extreme the way SM-2/Anki ease can drift into ease hell. Difficulty then modulates the stability update (higher D means smaller stability gains).

nodes.definition: Compute the FSRS stability update, the formula that encodes the spacing effect. After a successful review (G>=2): S'_r = S*(e^{w8}*(11-D)*S^{-w9}*(e^{w10*(1-R)}-1)*w15[if G=2]*w16[if G=4] + 1). Properties: the stability increase SInc = S'/S >= 1; SInc shrinks with higher D and higher S; SInc GROWS as R drops - reviewing a card whose recall has fallen yields a bigger durability gain, the spacing effect made mechanical; and for overdue-but-recalled cards the gain converges to an upper bound instead of growing linearly as SM-2/Anki do (bounded stability gain) [FACT - FSRS algorithm wiki]. After a lapse (G=1): S'_f = w11*D^{-w12}*((S+1)^{w13}-1)*e^{w14*(1-R)}. For same-day (short-term) reviews: S'(S,G) = S*e^{w17*(G-3+w18)}*S^{-w19}. Empirically the spacing effect this encodes is well attested (Rea & Modigliani 1985: 70% vs 53% distributed vs massed; Donovan & Radosevich 1999 meta-analysis effect size 0.46) [FACT - fetched FSRS tutorial].

nodes.definition: Establish desired retention r as the single workload knob, the decision that trades knowledge against review load. Interval = the inverse forgetting curve at r (I(r,S) from the curve node), so r is a direct dial on how often cards return. Anki's default is 0.90; the manual warns higher retention gives shorter intervals and more reviews per day, that above 90% workload increases very quickly, and above 97% it can be overwhelming [FACT - deck-options.md]. The workload-vs-retention relationship is U-shaped, not monotone: raising r shortens intervals and adds reviews, while lowering r causes more forgetting and more relearning, so there is a workload-MINIMIZING retention. Anki's CMRR (Compute Minimum Recommended Retention) searches for it, and going below it is dominated - more time AND less knowledge, where knowledge is approximately the sum of R across all cards [FACT - optimal-retention wiki + deck-options.md].

nodes.definition: Compose the choose-and-tune verdict the whole KB builds toward. Reconciled rules an expert applies: (1) log the revlog shape from day one no matter which scheduler runs, because it is the option-preserving prerequisite for any later optimization or migration; (2) prefer FSRS when the user has enough revlog to optimize and cares about efficiency, because it makes elapsed time first-class and bounds overdue gains where SM-2/Anki are ad hoc; (3) SM-2/classic-Anki remains a legitimate default for a cold start, a disciplined on-time reviewer, or when inspectability matters, since its single EF is hand-predictable; (4) never silently equate the 0-5 and 1-4 grade scales - reconcile only at import; (5) set exactly one workload knob (desired retention, default 0.90) and find its minimum with CMRR rather than stacking ad-hoc multipliers; (6) add fuzz to any homegrown scheduler; (7) refuse to quote an FSRS parameter, an SM-2 constant or a primary-source effect size the grounding file did not verify. A scheduler choice that skips revlog logging or mis-maps grades is a no-go until fixed.

included: the reconciled choose/tune rules across the three families
when to prefer FSRS vs SM-2/classic-Anki and the log-revlog-first and one-retention-knob mandates
the grade-mapping and no-fabricated-constant discipline
excluded: the per-family formula detail (their own nodes)
the storage/transport integration surface (excluded)

pros.claim: A single reconciled verdict prevents choosing a scheduler while grade-mapping or revlog-logging prerequisites are unmet
pros.example: withholding an FSRS go until the revlog is logged in the shape its optimizer consumes

cons.claim: A compact go/no-go can over-simplify a mixed collection where different decks warrant different schedulers or retention
cons.example: one verdict for a whole collection when a fast-moving language deck and a stable trivia deck want different retention targets

failure_modes: choosing a scheduler without logging the revlog shape and foreclosing later optimization
shipping a verdict that silently equates the 0-5 and 1-4 grade scales
acceptance_tests: the verdict states log-revlog-first, when to prefer FSRS vs SM-2/classic-Anki, the one-retention-knob-with-CMRR rule, add-fuzz, grade-mapping-only-at-import, and refuse-unverified-constants, and conditions any go on those prerequisites
revisit_triggers: a new scheduler family or FSRS version changes the choice
a user accumulates enough revlog to switch to FSRS
a grade-mapping or revlog-logging gap is found in an implementation

base.update_signal: a new scheduler, a revlog accumulation, or an implementation gap changes the verdict

edges.why_related: the grade input of the scheduler function is exactly what the grade vocabularies specify
the state output of the scheduler function is exactly what the per-family state models describe
the revlog records the grade in the 1-4 button vocabulary, so the vocabulary must be fixed first
the revlog records interval/last-interval state transitions the state model defines
the EF update is a function of the SM-2 quality grade q, so the 0-5 grade scale must be fixed first
EF is the SM-2 state component the update evolves
the ladder multiplies by EF from the third rung, so EF must be computed first
the failure reset restarts the ladder from I(1), so the ladder must be defined first
the precise failure semantics turn on the EF update still running on the failed repetition
the elapsed-time blindness is a property of the ladder multiplying the planned interval regardless of real delay
Anki's configurable learning steps replace the fixed 1d/6d rungs of the SM-2 ladder
Anki's flat ease deltas replace SM-2's quadratic EF formula, so the EF update is the baseline they modify
lapse handling operates on the review-card ease the deltas define
Anki's configurable New-Interval lapse softens SM-2's hard failure reset, so the reset is its baseline
the days-late credit is the patch that specifically addresses SM-2's elapsed-time blindness
the late-credit interval formula multiplies by the ease factor the deltas maintain
the Hard/Easy/modifier multipliers layer on top of the ease-scaled interval
fuzz is applied last, after the multipliers have produced the interval
the FSRS (D,S,R) model is the alternative state model contrasted against SM-2's
the forgetting curve computes R from S and elapsed time, the components the DSR model defines
the initial-state formulas seed the (D,S) the DSR model defines
the difficulty update evolves and mean-reverts toward the initial D0 the initial-state node sets
the stability update reads R from the forgetting curve in its (e^{w10*(1-R)}-1) spacing-effect term
the stability gain shrinks with difficulty D, so D must be updated before S
the optimizer fits the w-terms inside the stability formulas to the revlog
the optimizer consumes the logged revlog history, so the log shape must exist first
the retention knob sets r in the curve's inverse interval I(r,S), so the curve must be defined first
the classic-Anki interval-modifier identity is the SM-2-world approximation of the desired-retention knob
setting exactly one workload knob is a reconciled rule of the choose/tune verdict
whether the user has enough revlog to optimize is a condition for preferring FSRS in the verdict
add-fuzz-to-any-homegrown-scheduler is one of the verdict's reconciled rules
the lapse/leech handling is part of the classic-Anki behavior the verdict weighs against FSRS
SM-2's inspectable single-EF failure behavior is why it stays a legitimate cold-start default in the verdict
SM-2 ignores actual elapsed time while the FSRS curve makes it a first-class input, a direct design disagreement
edges.resolution_rule: when scheduling for irregular or overdue reviewers, prefer the FSRS curve that consumes elapsed time; keep SM-2 only for disciplined on-time reviewers where the blind spot rarely bites

edges.why_related: SM-2 lowers EF on every graded failure while Anki's learning phase deliberately shields ease from acquisition failures - opposite conventions
edges.resolution_rule: adopt Anki's ease-shield during the acquisition/learning phase to avoid low-interval hell, and apply the SM-2-style ease penalty only to post-graduation review failures

edges.why_related: Anki's monotone linear interval growth (>= prev+1 day, unbounded late credit) conflicts with FSRS's bounded stability gain for overdue cards
edges.resolution_rule: prefer FSRS's bounded stability gain when overdue reviews are common; use Anki's linear multipliers only as a simpler approximation when FSRS parameters cannot yet be fit

edges.why_related: both map a memory-strength state to a next interval - SM-2 via I(n)=I*EF, FSRS via I=S at R=0.9 - so they are the two answers to the same scheduling question
the stability produced by each review causally sets the interval the retention knob then evaluates at r

conflict_axes.name: elapsed_time_ignored_vs_first_class
conflict_axes.description: SM-2 schedules from (EF,n) and ignores actual elapsed time, while FSRS makes elapsed time a first-class input via R(t,S); Anki sits between with an ad-hoc days-late patch.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: prefer FSRS for irregular/overdue reviewers; SM-2 or Anki's days-late patch suffice only for disciplined on-time users

conflict_axes.name: failure_penalizes_ease_vs_shields_it
conflict_axes.description: SM-2 runs the EF-lowering update on every graded failure, while Anki deliberately shields ease during the learning/acquisition phase to avoid low-interval hell.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: shield ease in the learning phase and apply an ease penalty only to post-graduation review failures

conflict_axes.name: hard_reset_vs_partial_interval_on_lapse
conflict_axes.description: SM-2 hard-resets a lapsed card to I(1) while Anki keeps a configurable fraction via the New Interval multiplier.
poles: keep a fraction of the interval
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: use a non-zero New Interval to preserve hard-won interval unless the item is a genuine leech to be re-learned from scratch

conflict_axes.name: unbounded_linear_growth_vs_bounded_stability_gain
conflict_axes.description: Anki's linear multipliers and unbounded days-late credit can inflate intervals without limit, while FSRS bounds the stability gain of overdue-but-recalled cards.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: prefer FSRS's bounded gain when overdue reviews are common; treat Anki's linear growth as an approximation only

conflict_axes.name: coarse_flat_deltas_vs_smooth_quadratic_ease
conflict_axes.description: Anki's four flat ease deltas discard the failure-severity gradation SM-2's quadratic-in-(5-q) EF formula encodes.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: accept the coarser four-button table for simplicity and only reach for finer grading when a use case truly needs failure-severity resolution

conflict_axes.name: inspectable_single_ease_vs_trained_dsr
conflict_axes.description: SM-2/Anki's single hand-predictable EF trades against FSRS's more accurate but opaque trained (D,S) and 21 parameters.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: use SM-2/Anki when inspectability or a cold start matters; move to FSRS once enough revlog exists and accuracy matters more than transparency

conflict_axes.name: higher_retention_vs_lower_workload
conflict_axes.description: Raising desired retention shortens intervals and adds reviews while lowering it adds forgetting and relearning; the workload curve is U-shaped with an interior minimum.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: set retention at or near the CMRR workload minimum (default 0.90) rather than pushing toward 0.97 where workload blows up, and never below the minimum where the choice is dominated

conflict_axes.name: deterministic_schedule_vs_mandatory_fuzz
conflict_axes.description: A deterministic scheduler is reproducible and easy to test but clumps same-cohort cards into review spikes, which Anki's non-disableable fuzz deliberately prevents.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: add fuzz of Anki's magnitude to spread load and accept non-determinism, asserting intervals within the fuzz band rather than exactly in tests

conflict_axes.name: default_parameters_vs_personal_optimization
conflict_axes.description: FSRS default parameters give an immediate cold-start schedule but only a per-user revlog fit personalizes the forgetting curve, at the cost of needing data and risking overfit.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: start on defaults, log the revlog from day one, and reoptimize about once a month with an Ignore-before date to exclude stale habits

edge_cases.description: An implementation runs the SM-2 ladder reset on a failure but skips the step-5 EF update, so EF never drops on lapses
edge_cases.trigger: the reader treats 'EF unchanged on reset' as 'EF unchanged on failure'
edge_cases.mitigation: run the EF update on every repetition including failures, and separately reset the ladder position on q<3

edge_cases.description: The canonical SM-2 formula cannot be verified against supermemo.com because the page is unreachable this session (egress 403)
edge_cases.trigger: someone asks to confirm the EF formula against the original SuperMemo page rather than the mirrors
edge_cases.mitigation: carry the FACT-by-cross-match-against-26-mirrors basis and the named egress blocker, and re-verify when supermemo.com becomes reachable

edge_cases.description: An SM-2 log is imported into Anki by equating q=3 with Good and q=0 with Again, corrupting the ease trajectory
edge_cases.trigger: the 0-5 and 1-4 grade scales are equated outside an explicit import mapping
edge_cases.mitigation: define an explicit lossy import mapping at the boundary and never equate the scales in live scheduling

edge_cases.description: A homegrown deterministic scheduler introduces 200 cards on one day and they all fall due together weeks later
edge_cases.trigger: intervals are computed with no fuzz so a same-day cohort clumps
edge_cases.mitigation: add banded fuzz of Anki's magnitude (+/- 1 day + 15%/10%/5%) so cohorts spread across days

edge_cases.description: An FSRS forgetting curve is coded with the wrong factor so R(S,S) does not equal 0.9 and every interval is mis-timed
edge_cases.mitigation: assert R(S,S)=0.9 as a unit invariant and derive factor from the closed form, not a hardcoded constant

edge_cases.description: The FSRS success stability formula is applied to a lapse (G=1) instead of the lapse formula, over-rewarding a failure
edge_cases.trigger: the G>=2 branch is taken for G=1
edge_cases.mitigation: branch on grade: use S'_f = w11*D^{-w12}*((S+1)^{w13}-1)*e^{w14*(1-R)} for G=1 and the success form only for G>=2

edge_cases.description: A user or tool hand-edits or copies another user's FSRS parameters, degrading scheduling
edge_cases.trigger: parameters are pasted between presets/users against the manual's advice
edge_cases.mitigation: never hand-edit or copy parameters; run Optimize on the user's own revlog and reoptimize about monthly

edge_cases.description: FSRS is reoptimized on a few weeks of imported logs from a different study habit and overfits, mis-scheduling going forward
edge_cases.trigger: reoptimization runs over stale or foreign revlog without an Ignore-before date
edge_cases.mitigation: set the 'Ignore cards reviewed before' date to exclude stale habits/imported logs and require sufficient recent revlog

edge_cases.description: A learner pushes desired retention to 0.97 for safety and is buried in reviews the U-curve shows is far past the workload minimum
edge_cases.trigger: retention is treated as strictly-better-when-higher, ignoring the workload blow-up above 0.90
edge_cases.mitigation: set retention at or near the CMRR minimum (default 0.90) and treat above-0.90 as a steep workload trade

edge_cases.description: A study system logs only grade and new interval, then finds the FSRS optimizer cannot reconstruct recall-vs-forget sequences
edge_cases.trigger: the revlog is captured with fewer fields than the optimizer consumes
edge_cases.mitigation: log the full tuple (timestamp, item, grade 1-4, interval, last_interval, duration, type) from day one

edge_cases.description: An answer cites a primary-source effect size (Ebbinghaus figures, Cepeda 2006 or Roediger 2006 exact percentages) as fetched fact
edge_cases.trigger: an UNKNOWN primary-source number is quoted as verified
edge_cases.mitigation: hold those exact numbers UNKNOWN (journals/Wikipedia blocked this session); cite only the two fetched findings (Rea & Modigliani 70% vs 53%, Donovan & Radosevich effect size 0.46)

edge_cases.description: A card recalled very late on Easy inflates its Anki interval far beyond what memory science supports because days-late credit is unbounded
edge_cases.trigger: a hugely overdue Easy review multiplies an already-inflated interval
edge_cases.mitigation: cap with the Maximum Interval and prefer FSRS's bounded stability gain when overdue reviews are common

workflow.action: Frame the scheduler as a (grade, elapsed) function and fix the grade vocabularies and state models
workflow.description: State the (grade, elapsed) -> (state, interval) signature, the SM-2 0-5 vs Anki/FSRS 1-4 scales, and the SM-2 (EF,n) vs FSRS (D,S) state
workflow.gate: the signature, both grade scales and both state models are stated with the reconcile-only-at-import rule

workflow.action: Commit to logging the revlog shape from day one
workflow.description: Specify the (timestamp, item, grade 1-4, interval, last_interval, duration, type) tuple and why it enables optimization, import and benchmarking
workflow.gate: the full revlog tuple and its three enabling reasons are stated

workflow.action: Compute the SM-2 EF update and interval ladder
workflow.description: Give the EF formula, floor 1.3, per-grade deltas and the I(1)=1/I(2)=6/I(n)=I*EF ladder with round-up
workflow.gate: the EF formula with floor, the six deltas and the ladder are stated with the supermemo.com-unreachable caveat

workflow.action: Specify SM-2 failure handling and elapsed-time blindness
workflow.description: State q<3 resets the ladder without the reset changing EF, that EF still drops, and that SM-2 ignores elapsed time
workflow.gate: the reset-vs-EF separation and the elapsed-time blind spot are stated

workflow.action: Model classic Anki's deviations (learning steps, ease deltas, lapse/leech)
workflow.description: Give the learning steps and ease-shield, the flat deltas and floor, and the New-Interval lapse and leech handling
workflow.gate: the learning-step ease shield, the flat deltas with floor 1.3, and the New-Interval/leech lapse are stated

workflow.action: Model Anki's elapsed-time patch, multipliers and mandatory fuzz
workflow.description: Give the days-late credit formulas, Hard/Easy/modifier/cap multipliers with the log-ratio identity, and the non-disableable banded fuzz
workflow.gate: the days-late formulas, the multipliers with the interval-modifier identity, and the fuzz bands are stated

workflow.action: Establish the FSRS DSR model and power forgetting curve
workflow.description: Define D, S, R and give R(t,S) with factor and the inverse interval I(r,S)
workflow.gate: D/S/R are defined and the power curve with factor and its inverse are stated with R(S,S)=0.9

workflow.action: Compute FSRS initial state and difficulty/stability updates
workflow.description: Give S0(G)=w[G-1], D0, the mean-reverting difficulty update, and the success/lapse/same-day stability forms with bounded gain and spacing effect
workflow.gate: the initial state, difficulty update and the three stability forms are stated with SInc>=1 and bounded overdue gain

workflow.action: Fit the 21 parameters to the user's revlog
workflow.description: State the MLE binary log-loss fit over the revlog, per-preset params, monthly reoptimization and the Ignore-before date
workflow.gate: the w-vector fit to the revlog by log-loss, per-preset scope and the reoptimization/Ignore-before advice are stated

workflow.action: Set desired retention as the single workload knob
workflow.description: State interval = inverse curve at r, the default 0.90 and above-0.97 overwhelm, the U-shaped workload curve and CMRR
workflow.gate: the retention knob, the U-shaped workload curve, CMRR and the dominated-below-minimum rule are stated

workflow.description: State log-revlog-first, FSRS-vs-SM-2 choice, one-retention-knob-with-CMRR, add-fuzz, grade-mapping and no-fabricated-constants rules
workflow.gate: the verdict conditions any go on revlog logging and correct grade mapping and applies the reconciled rules

dominance_rules.rule: The honesty label dominates any algorithm constant or effect size
dominance_rules.rationale: the SM-2 page was unreachable and primary psychology effect sizes were blocked, so nothing may be quoted as fetched fact unless the grounding file verified it
dominance_rules.trigger: an FSRS parameter, SM-2 constant or study effect size is stated
dominance_rules.action: quote only grounding-verified values, carry the supermemo.com-unreachable and primary-source-UNKNOWN caveats, and never invent a number

dominance_rules.rule: Elapsed-time-aware scheduling dominates elapsed-blind scheduling for irregular reviewers
dominance_rules.rationale: SM-2 gives the same next interval whether on time or a month late, which mis-schedules overdue-heavy users
dominance_rules.trigger: the target user reviews irregularly or often overdue
dominance_rules.action: prefer FSRS's R(t,S) curve, or at minimum Anki's days-late credit, over the raw SM-2 ladder

dominance_rules.rule: The bounded FSRS stability gain dominates unbounded linear late credit when overdue reviews are common
dominance_rules.rationale: unbounded days-late credit can inflate an interval past what memory science supports
dominance_rules.trigger: a very overdue card would multiply an inflated interval
dominance_rules.action: prefer FSRS's bounded gain or apply the Maximum Interval cap to the Anki result

dominance_rules.rule: Logging the full revlog shape dominates any minimal logging convenience
dominance_rules.rationale: a grade-only log can never be optimized or migrated later
dominance_rules.trigger: a scheduler is about to log fewer fields than the revlog tuple
dominance_rules.action: log the full (timestamp, item, grade 1-4, interval, last_interval, duration, type) tuple from day one

dominance_rules.rule: The CMRR workload minimum dominates a naive higher-is-safer retention
dominance_rules.rationale: workload is U-shaped and rises steeply above 0.90, becoming overwhelming above 0.97, while below the minimum is strictly dominated
dominance_rules.trigger: desired retention is set above the CMRR minimum for safety or below it to save time
dominance_rules.action: set retention at or near the CMRR minimum (default 0.90) and treat above-0.90 as a steep trade

dominance_rules.rule: The learning-phase ease shield dominates the SM-2 failed-repetition ease penalty during acquisition
dominance_rules.rationale: penalizing ease on early stumbles causes low-interval hell
dominance_rules.trigger: an ease penalty is about to apply to a learning-phase failure
dominance_rules.action: shield ease during learning and apply the ease penalty only to post-graduation review failures

dominance_rules.rule: Explicit import-boundary grade mapping dominates silent scale equation
dominance_rules.rationale: equating 0-5 with 1-4 anywhere but an import step corrupts the ease/EF math
dominance_rules.trigger: two grade scales meet outside an explicit import mapping
dominance_rules.action: map the scales only at the import boundary and keep each family on its own scale in live scheduling

dominance_rules.rule: Per-user optimized parameters dominate hand-edited or copied parameters
dominance_rules.rationale: the manual warns hand-edited or copied parameters degrade scheduling
dominance_rules.trigger: FSRS parameters are about to be pasted between users or presets
dominance_rules.action: run Optimize on the user's own revlog and reoptimize about monthly instead of copying parameters

anti_rework_rules.rule: Log the full revlog tuple from day one before building any scheduling on top of it
anti_rework_rules.prevents: discovering later that a grade-only log cannot train FSRS or import into Anki, forcing a re-instrumentation

anti_rework_rules.rule: Fix each family's grade scale and map only at import boundaries before wiring ease/EF math
anti_rework_rules.prevents: a silent 0-5 to 1-4 mismatch corrupting every downstream ease update and a full rescheduling redo

anti_rework_rules.rule: Run the SM-2 EF update on every repetition including failures when first implementing it
anti_rework_rules.prevents: a lapse-EF bug where failures never lower EF, caught only after cards mis-schedule

anti_rework_rules.rule: Branch the FSRS stability update on grade (lapse vs success) at implementation time
anti_rework_rules.prevents: applying the success formula to a lapse and over-rewarding failures, found only in a benchmark later

anti_rework_rules.rule: Derive the forgetting-curve factor from 0.9^(-1/w20)-1 and assert R(S,S)=0.9 as a unit test
anti_rework_rules.prevents: a wrong-factor curve mis-timing every interval and needing a full re-derivation after release

anti_rework_rules.rule: Add banded fuzz to a homegrown scheduler from the start
anti_rework_rules.prevents: same-cohort cards clumping into review spikes that require re-spreading the whole backlog

anti_rework_rules.rule: Set the Ignore-before date and require sufficient recent revlog before reoptimizing FSRS
anti_rework_rules.prevents: overfitting to stale or imported logs and having to discard the fitted parameters

anti_rework_rules.rule: Choose the retention target at the CMRR minimum before committing a study plan
anti_rework_rules.prevents: setting an overwhelming above-0.97 target and having to rebuild the schedule after burnout

iteration_protocol.trigger: a user accumulates enough new revlog that a reoptimization would meaningfully move the parameters
iteration_protocol.action: run the FSRS optimizer on the recent revlog, refit w0..w20, and re-derive the retention/workload minimum

iteration_protocol.trigger: the canonical supermemo.com SM-2 page becomes reachable and the EF formula can be verified directly
iteration_protocol.action: verify the EF update and interval ladder against the original page and drop or update the unreachable-page caveat

iteration_protocol.trigger: a new FSRS version (beyond FSRS-6) changes the formulas, the parameter count or the default vector
iteration_protocol.action: update the DSR model, forgetting curve, initial-state and stability nodes and re-check the 21-parameter references

iteration_protocol.trigger: Anki changes a default (learning steps, ease deltas, New Interval, multipliers, fuzz bands or the CMRR method)
iteration_protocol.action: update the affected classic-Anki node and re-check the retention-knob approximation

iteration_protocol.trigger: primary-source psychology effect sizes (Ebbinghaus, Cepeda 2006, Roediger 2006) become fetchable
iteration_protocol.action: replace the UNKNOWN-tagged exact figures with fetched values and re-cite the spacing/testing-effect basis

iteration_protocol.trigger: a study system's revlog is found to log fewer fields than the optimizer consumes
iteration_protocol.action: extend the logging to the full tuple and re-confirm the optimization and Anki-import paths

iteration_protocol.trigger: an overdue-heavy usage pattern or an interval-inflation report tests the elapsed-time handling
iteration_protocol.action: re-evaluate SM-2 blindness vs Anki days-late vs FSRS bounded gain for that user and update the verdict

priority_rationale: The framing nodes (scheduler-as-function, grade vocabularies, memory-state models, revlog logging) come first because every algorithm and tuning choice is read against that shared interface and the option-preserving log; the SM-2 core (EF update, interval ladder, failure reset, elapsed blindness) next because it is the oldest family and the baseline the others deviate from; the classic-Anki deviations then patch that baseline (learning steps, ease deltas, lapse/leech, days-late credit, multipliers, fuzz); the FSRS DSR stack (model, forgetting curve, initial state, difficulty and stability updates, parameter optimization) then supplies the modern compute core that makes elapsed time first-class; and the desired-retention knob and the choose-and-tune verdict come last because they compose every upstream family into a single workload decision and a defensible scheduler selection.
